a1_answer:
NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
Propose a mitigation for biuret formation by retuning the vacuum setpoint to lower the operating temperature and adjusting the feed-ratio to minimize residence time. Standard practice maintains a fixed high vacuum (low pressure) which lowers the boiling point but fails to account for the cumulative thermal load on the melt over extended batch times, or it uses a fixed feed rate that maximizes throughput at the cost of extended dwell. This mitigation is a genuine departure because it decouples the temperature reduction (via deeper vacuum) from the throughput constraint, instead using the feed-ratio to shorten the effective residence time of the bulk melt within the critical temperature window, rather than just lowering the temperature for its own sake. Adjacent-technique clearance: In polymer processing, similar "short-shot" or pulsed feed strategies are used to minimize degradation; here, it is applied to a continuous film evaporator by modulating the feed-mass-flow-rate relative to the evaporation capacity, a parameter change not typically tuned as a primary biuret inhibitor. The mechanism attacks the failure's driving physics by simultaneously reducing the thermal energy input (lower T) and the time integration of that energy (shorter effective τ), breaking the equilibrium trap where biuret concentration rises with both T and τ.

PHYSICS CHECK
DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = cumulative thermal dose (∫T·dt over residence); the mechanism moves it down by lowering T (via increased vacuum) and reducing effective residence time (via feed-ratio retuning); this reduces the biuret formation rate. Biuret formation follows a pseudo-first-order reaction where rate k(T) ≈ A exp(-Ea/RT). Lowering T from 135°C to ~125°C (achievable by deepening vacuum from e.g., 5 kPa to 3 kPa for urea) reduces k by a factor of ~2-3 (Arrhenius, Ea ~ 100 kJ/mol for urea decomposition). Reducing residence time by 50% (via feed-ratio increase relative to evap capacity, thinning the film or reducing bulk holdup) halves the integral ∫k dt. Combined, the biuret yield is reduced by ~40-60%, breaking the quality limit.
INPUT-AVAILABILITY: The mechanism requires online signals: Vacuum pressure (stated in constraint "vacuum setpoint") and Feed rate (stated in "feed-ratio retuning"). Both are permitted and standard in the stated infrastructure. No new instrumentation is needed.
COST-PRICING: Deepening vacuum reduces evaporation capacity per unit area, potentially lowering throughput by ~10-15% if not compensated. However, the feed-ratio retuning (increasing feed rate relative to evap capacity) thins the film, reducing viscosity and heat load, which may offset some energy cost. The net operational cost is a small decrease in energy input (lower T) but a potential decrease in maximum stable throughput. The trade is positive because biuret rejection costs (quality loss, reprocessing) are far higher than the small energy/throughput penalty. Explicit operational loss: ~5-10% reduction in maximum sustainable throughput during the tuned window, zero loss outside it.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
MECHANISM CLASS: Setpoint/Procedure Retuning
(a) Set the existing vacuum controller setpoint from 5 kPa to 3 kPa (standard controller parameter change, no hardware).
(c) Retune the feed-pump speed or feed-valve opening to increase the feed-rate-to-evaporation-capacity ratio by 20% (procedure change on existing pump/valve, no hardware).
(c) Define a new operating procedure: hold the 3 kPa setpoint for the entire batch, and maintain the 20% higher feed ratio for the first 80% of the batch, then revert to standard ratio for the final 20% to prevent under-evaporation. This is a procedural schedule, no hardware.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
(a) Vacuum controller setpoint change: Zero cost, zero installation burden. Same class as standard setpoint adjustment. Operational loss: 0 (pure parameter).
(c) Feed-ratio retuning: Zero cost, zero installation burden. Same class as standard feed adjustment. Operational loss: ~5% throughput reduction during tuned window (priced above). Net burden: same-or-lower than standard practice (no new hardware, no maintenance, same operator skill level).
(c) New procedure schedule: Zero cost. Burden: minimal operator training. Same class as existing SOPs. No new hardware. Parity: same-or-lower.
EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Run two identical batches under standard conditions (5 kPa, standard feed ratio) and two under the mitigated conditions (3 kPa, 20% higher feed ratio for 80% of batch). Measure biuret content via standard HPLC or titration at end-of-batch. Pass/fail threshold: Mitigated batch biuret content < 50% of standard batch biuret content. Duration: 4 full batch cycles (2 per condition) to establish statistical significance. Kill criterion: If mitigated batch biuret content does not drop by >30% within 4 cycles, the mechanism is falsified; revert to standard practice.
